title: Midnight songs (Acts 16:16–40)
hookLine: a slave girl freed, a beating, prison, hymns, an earthquake, a jailer baptized
tomorrow: who checks a preacher's homework, and why does Acts praise them?

cards: Three in the morning is the loneliest hour for a worried mind. Some people scroll. Some pace the kitchen.
In Philippi, Paul sets a slave girl free from the spirit her owners profited from, and they see "that the hope of their gains was gone."
So Paul and Silas are dragged before the magistrates, beaten, and locked in the inner prison, feet fastened in the stocks. And at midnight?
"And at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them." They sing.

teach.b: Then an earthquake. The doors open, every prisoner's bands come loose, and the jailer, sure his prisoners have fled, is about to harm himself. Paul calls out in the dark: "Do thyself no harm: for we are all here."
He brings a light, comes in trembling, and asks, "Sirs, what must I do to be saved?" Before dawn the jailer has washed their wounds and fed them at his own table, and his household is baptized.
If a dark hour like that is yours right now, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number. So is singing the faithful thing in a hard hour? Christians hold two honest views.

teach.h: VIEW ONE: PRAISE IN THE DARK.
teach.b: Praise in the dark is faith at its bravest, and the other prisoners heard it. Paul later writes, "Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice." The second: not always, and not on command.
The Bible keeps sad songs too.

teach.h: VIEW TWO: HARPS ON THE WILLOWS.
teach.b: In Psalm 137, exiles say, "We hanged our harps upon the willows," and ask, "How shall we sing the LORD'S song in a strange land?"
Christians who hold this view say lament is prayer too, and forced cheer can bury real grief. Here's the detail both sides can use: Acts never says what they sang.
It says they prayed and sang.
The hurt and the song, in the same cell.

how: Christians sing hymns and psalms in hard hours as well as glad ones, at home, at bedsides and in church, and some churches also pray the psalms of lament.

o: songs sung in a prison cell at the darkest hour
night songs the temple guards sang on watch
hymns written for a Christmas midnight service

games.q: midnight in Philippi — tap the pairs.
p: the hope of their gains was gone

s: the songs opened the prison doors
Acts says an earthquake opened them. the songs were already rising.
Acts tells us which hymn they sang
it says they prayed and sang praises, not what.
the Bible keeps sad songs as well as glad ones
Psalm 137: we hanged our harps upon the willows.

games.q: your choir is asked to sing the week a classmate died. one alto wants only bright, hopeful songs. another wants a sad psalm. what's the best case for the sad one?
o: grief sung honestly is still prayer; the Bible keeps those songs.
sad songs show the singers have quietly given up on God.
Paul and Silas sang only cheerful songs, so sad ones are a break.
games.why: that's the lament view at its best: Psalm 137 is in the Bible too. the praise view answers with a midnight cell. both are Christian voices.

practice: Hum or sing one line of a song you know by heart, softly, once or a few times, in whatever key the day is in: glad, tired or sad. It doesn't need to sound good; it only needs to be yours.
If singing isn't for you, listen to the room instead, the way the prisoners listened.

wordCard.voice: Midnight songs. Paul and Silas, beaten and locked in the stocks, praying and singing while the prisoners listened.

orig.note: Greek: they sang praises, the verb in Acts 16:25.

carryVoice: The line to keep: at midnight they sang, before anything at all had changed. Until tomorrow.
